reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The most concrete measured picture of government AI use in this material comes from GAO's audit of federal agencies. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those reported use cases were still in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported that they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases.

What agencies say they are doing with it is narrow and operational. GAO lists analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, along with agencies using AI operationally to identify information security threats and to facilitate the review of large datasets. On money, GAO reports that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI.

GAO also documents the governance gap. It found no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and it found that five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported use cases while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, with two inventories including AI uses later determined by the agencies not to be AI. On compliance, ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence, while the Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, the Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements.

Stanford HAI frames the same problem at a higher level. Its AI Index describes a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating, and adoption spreading while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology fall behind, in a field where data transparency is declining. Stanford HAI notes the Index has been referenced by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union, and it points to a sharp increase in AI adoption in medicine, including clinical documentation, medical imaging, and diagnostic reasoning. It also describes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez of The Hague University of Applied Sciences on a judicial decision database intended to improve predictability and legal certainty for providers and users of AI.

The cross-national policy picture is tracked by two organizations here. OECD.AI, the OECD Artificial Intelligence Policy Observatory, says it helps countries shape trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles and gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, with organisations developing advanced AI systems able to participate by submitting a report to facilitate transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures, and with the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work joined under the GPAI brand. Oxford Insights says it helps governments increase the impact of their public services by empowering teams and harnessing technology, and its Government AI Readiness Index scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption.

The regulatory posture is where this site's own tracking is most specific. Its AI laws section reports 6,003 artificial intelligence bills tracked across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database, and a comparison of 103 measures across 27 states reviewed on September 18, 2026, which found that no two states wrote the same law. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149, while every other measure names one setting such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom, or a state agency. Where the stakes are personal, the recurring rule is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider: insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law, the attorney general enforces the larger laws often exclusively, and several states simply declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a few practical conclusions. The federal record shows that most reported government use cases are still planned rather than in production, that inventories are frequently incomplete, and that acquisition guidance is missing, so internal record keeping and lifecycle tracking are the weak points to plan for. The state record shows that the question in each state is never whether you use AI but what you use it for, and that building to the common core, telling people when they are dealing with AI, keeping a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits, or education, having a crisis protocol and knowing the age of your user if your product holds a conversation, and keeping records of what the system does, covers the duties that recur most often, with the attorney general as the enforcer you are most likely to meet.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI describes itself as a policy observatory that helps countries shape trustworthy AI in line with the OECD AI Principles, and says it offers access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog on AI policy. It invites organisations developing advanced AI systems to take part by submitting a report, saying that sharing information would help make risk mitigation measures more transparent and comparable. The observatory states that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI combined under the GPAI brand into one integrated partnership. Its stated purpose is to help AI actors build and use systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
